title: Painted sakhis
hookLine: sakhis became paintings, murals and later posters in Sikh homes
tomorrow: Telling a sakhi to a child

lines: AN OLD MAN UNDER A TREE.
cards: In a living room in Birmingham, or Fresno, or Ludhiana, there's a framed picture above the sofa. An old man with a white beard sits under a tree. On one side, a younger man holds a stringed instrument.
On the other, a man waves a whisk over him. A child in that house has looked at it every day since before she could read. Ask her who they are, and she'll tell you.
Nobody sat her down for a lesson. The wall did it.

teach.b: On day seven hundred twenty-six we met B40, a book with a painting beside each sakhi. A book sits on a shelf, and someone has to open it. Today the pictures leave the book.
Sakhis went up on walls: murals painted inside gurdwaras and old houses, showing Nanak on the road, at the river, with the yogis on the mountain.
Later came printed pictures, posters and calendars, cheap enough to hang in any home. That changes how a picture teaches. A page is seen when you sit down to read it.

A wall is seen over and over without trying: on the way to breakfast, in the middle of an argument, on a sick day on the sofa. The girl in that living room never had a lesson. She had years of passing by.
Look closer at her picture. The man with the whisk is Bhai Bala, the companion from the Bala tellings, the one historians still discuss. A print has no footnotes.
It quietly carries one telling's choices into the house, and its faces are each artist's own imagining.
So yesterday's habit works on walls too: ask what the picture knows, and which telling it comes from. Sikh teachers add a caution.

teach.h: A REMINDER, NOT AN OBJECT OF WORSHIP.
teach.b: A picture is a reminder of a story, not something to bow to.
In the gurdwara, the bow goes to the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word. The picture points; it doesn't receive.

how: Sikh homes and gurdwaras may display paintings and prints of scenes from the Gurus' lives as reminders of the stories, while the bow in the gurdwara is made to the Guru Granth Sahib.

paintings Sikhs bow to in the gurdwara

s: a print of a sakhi is a neutral record of what happened
it carries one telling's choices, like Bala at Nanak's side, and faces each artist imagined.
a picture on a wall can teach without anyone giving a lesson
the girl learned the scene by passing it every day.
in the gurdwara, Sikhs bow to the pictures of the Gurus
the bow goes to the Guru Granth Sahib; a picture is a reminder of a story.

games.q: a friend looks at the print above your sofa and says historians aren't sure Bala was ever with Nanak. what do you do?
o: take the picture down; it can't be trusted.
keep it, and know which telling it comes from.
insist Bala was there on every journey.
games.why: a print carries a telling's choices. the habit from yesterday works on walls too: ask what the picture knows, and where it comes from.

practice: Look at a picture near you, a family photo, a print, a child's drawing on the fridge, or your phone's lock screen if the walls are bare. Ask what moment someone chose to keep, and what it teaches anyone who passes it every day.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath.

wordCard.voice: Painted sakhis. Stories of the Gurus carried in pictures: on book pages, on walls, and in printed pictures in homes.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: a picture or painting.

carryVoice: Your line: pictures teach. A wall can teach without a word. Day seven hundred forty-four.
